bib.title: Multiple Testing (Chapter 13, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, with Applications in Python)
bib.venue: Springer Texts in Statistics (Springer Nature Switzerland AG), book chapter

question: How should hypothesis tests be interpreted and corrected when a very large number of null hypotheses are tested at once?
contributions: Reviews hypothesis testing, Type I/II errors and p-values (13.1).
Explains why testing many hypotheses inflates false rejections (13.2).
Presents FWER control by Bonferroni, Holm, Tukey and Scheffe (13.3).
Presents permutation-based p-values and plug-in FDR (13.5), with a Python lab (13.6).

results.claim: With m=100 independent true nulls tested each at alpha=0.05, the FWER is about 0.994.
results.setup: m independent tests, all nulls true, each rejected at p<alpha; FWER = 1-(1-alpha)^m (Eq 13.5).
results.quote: taking α = 0.05 leads to a FWER of 1 −(1 −0.05)100 = 0.994

results.claim: Testing m=10,000 true nulls at alpha=0.01 gives about 100 expected false rejections.
results.setup: All m nulls true, per-test threshold alpha=0.01, expected count = alpha x m.
results.quote:
If m =
10,000, then that means that we expect to falsely reject 100 null hypotheses
by chance!
results.note: Quote line-break as printed in the text.

results.claim: Stockbroker/coin example: among 1,024 fair coins flipped ten times, one is expected to come up all tails, giving a p-value below 0.002 for that coin.
results.setup: Two-sided test that a coin is fair; 2/1,024 for ten heads or ten tails.
results.quote:
a
standard hypothesis test for the null hypothesis that this particular coin
is fair would lead to a p-value below 0.002!

results.claim: Controlling the FWER at 0.02 over 10 tests needs a per-test p threshold of 0.002, i.e. a test-statistic cutpoint of 3.09 instead of 2.33.
results.setup: Two-sample t-statistics with N(0,1) null; single-test Type I error 0.02 corresponds to |T|>=2.33.
results.quote:
This corresponds to a much more
stringent cutpoint of 3.09

results.claim: Bonferroni at FWER 0.05 over the first 5 Fund managers (threshold 0.05/5 = 0.01) rejects only Manager One; unadjusted alpha=0.05 rejects One and Three.
results.setup: Fund dataset, first 5 of 2,000 managers, n=50 monthly excess returns, one-sample t-test of mean=0; p-values 0.006, 0.918, 0.012, 0.601, 0.756.
results.quote:
we must control the Type
I error for each individual manager at level α/m = 0.05/5 = 0.01.

results.claim: Holm at FWER 0.05 on the same five p-values rejects Managers One and Three, one more than Bonferroni (thresholds 0.01 and 0.0125 passed, 0.601 > 0.0167 stops).
results.setup: Same Fund first-5 data; ordered p 0.006, 0.012, 0.601, 0.756, 0.918; alpha=0.05.
results.note: The prose says Holm 'rejects the first two null hypotheses' (by order) and then 'the first and third managers' (by manager); both describe the same two rejections.

results.claim: Holm is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni and makes no independence assumption, so the book says it should always be preferred.
results.setup: Any m p-values, any dependence; both control FWER at level alpha.
results.note: Text: 'uniformly more powerful than the Bonferroni method ... and so it should always be preferred.'

results.claim: Simulated m=10 tests with m0=2 true nulls: Bonferroni threshold is 0.005 at FWER 0.05; Holm rejects 0, 1 and 5 more false nulls than Bonferroni in the three panels (left, center, right), and neither makes a Type I error.
results.setup: Three simulated datasets; FWER controlled at 0.05.
results.quote: it rejects five more null hypotheses.
results.note: Fig 13.3 caption: center panel one more; right panel five more.

results.claim: Managers One and Two compared after peeking: unadjusted p=0.0349 (text) but Bonferroni over m=10 pairwise tests requires p<0.005, so the difference is not significant.
results.setup: Fund first 5 managers; alpha=0.05; 5x4/2=10 implicit comparisons.
results.quote:
A two-sample t-test
(13.1) for H0 yields a p-value of 0.0349
results.note: The lab (Sec 13.6.2) reports a paired t-test p-value of 0.038 for the same pair; Tukey adjusted p is 0.1862.

results.claim: Tukey's method adjusts the pairwise p of Managers One and Two from 0.038 to 0.186, so no pairwise difference is significant at FWER 0.05.
results.setup: Lab, pairwise_tukeyhsd on first 5 Fund managers, FWER=0.05.
results.quote:
the p-value for the difference between Managers One and Two
has increased from 0.038 to 0.186

results.claim: Scheffe's method requires alpha_S = 0.002 to keep Type I error at 0.05 for the post-hoc contrast (mu1+mu3)/2 vs (mu2+mu4+mu5)/3, so the unadjusted p=0.004 is not rejected.
results.setup: Fund first 5 managers, contrast chosen after seeing the data, alpha=0.05; same threshold applies to any split of the managers into two groups.
results.quote: we must set αS = 0.002.

results.claim: In the simulation (90% true nulls), power at FWER 0.05 is about 60% for m=10 and below 0.2 for m=500.
results.unit: fraction of false nulls rejected (upper bound for m=500)
results.setup: Simulation, 90% of m nulls true, 10% false; power = S/(m-m0). Values for m=10 and m=500 stated in text, curves in Fig 13.5.
results.quote:
With m = 500,
the power is below 0.2 at a FWER of 0.05
results.note: Setup details of the simulation (effect size, n) are not given.

results.claim: Controlling FDR at q=0.2 in the genomic example guarantees that on average at most 20% of genes followed up are false positives; p<0.05 alone would flag about 1,000 of 20,000 null genes.
results.setup: Hypothetical gene-association study; no genes truly associated.
results.quote:
we would expect 1,000 genes to have such small p-values
simply by chance

results.claim: BH at q=0.05 on the five-manager p-values rejects managers One and Three, matching Holm.
results.note: The number 0.02 is derived (0.05 x 2/5); the printed text contains the inequality only.

results.claim: BH guarantees FDR <= q if the m p-values are independent or only mildly dependent, whatever the number of true nulls.
results.setup: Algorithm 13.2; proof not given ('well beyond the scope').

results.claim: On all 2,000 Fund managers, BH at FDR 10% rejects 146 nulls, while Bonferroni at FWER 0.1 rejects none.
results.setup: One-sample t-test of mean return=0 per manager, n=50 months; statsmodels multipletests method fdr_bh vs p <= 0.1/2000.
results.quote: We find that 146 of the 2,000 fund managers have a q-value below 0.1
results.note: Fig 13.6 caption also gives 146; text says about 15 (10% of 146) expected false discoveries.

results.claim: At FDR 0.3 BH rejects 279 managers (about 83.7 expected false), while Bonferroni at FWER 0.3 rejects 1; 13 managers have raw p<0.001.
results.setup: Fund data, full 2,000 managers; Bonferroni baseline at FWER 0.3.
results.quote:
we can conclude that 279 fund managers are beating the market: we expect
that no more than around 279×0.3 = 83.7

results.claim: Permutation vs theoretical p-value for Khan gene 11 are nearly identical: t52 gives 0.041, 10,000 permutations give 0.042 (T=-2.09).
results.setup: Khan data, rhabdomyosarcoma vs Burkitt's lymphoma, two-sample t-test, gene 11.
results.quote: then we obtain a p-value of 0.042.
results.note: Lab permutation run prints 0.0398 and theoretical 0.0412 (Sec 13.6.4), because of a different random run.

results.claim: For Khan gene 877 (one extreme observation, skewed) theoretical and permutation null distributions differ: p=0.571 vs 0.673 (T=-0.57).
results.setup: Khan gene 877, same two-sample t-test setting.
results.quote: The theoretical p-value equals 0.571, and the re-sampling p-value equals 0.673.

results.claim: Plug-in permutation FDR (Algorithm 13.4, B=10,000) and BH on theoretical p-values give almost the same FDR curve on 2,308 Khan genes; the 500 smallest-p genes give FDR about 17.7%.
results.setup: Khan, rhabdomyosarcoma vs Burkitt's lymphoma, two-sample t-statistics, B=10,000.
results.quote:
rejecting the null hypothesis for the 500 genes with
the smallest p-values corresponds to an FDR of around 17.7%.

results.claim: Lab simulation (100 variables, 10 obs, 50 with mean 0.5): at alpha=0.05 the test makes V=5 false rejections and S=15 true rejections; with mean 1 it makes 2 and 40.
results.setup: One-sample t-tests, unit variance, unadjusted alpha=0.05; crosstab gives U=45, W=35 for mean 0.5; 2/40/48/10 for mean 1.
results.quote:
we reject 15 of the 50 false null hypotheses,
and we incorrectly reject 5 of the true null hypotheses.

results.claim: Lab subset FDR on 100 random Khan genes: FDR 0.1 rejects 15 genes, FDR 0.2 rejects 28.
results.setup: Random subset of Khan genes (rng.choice), plug-in permutation FDR.
results.quote:
with FDR controlled at 0.1, we reject 15 of the 100 null
hypotheses.
results.note: Subset depends on the random draw; Fig 13.11 shows the curve.

limits: Bonferroni and Holm hold under any dependence; BH needs independent or only mildly dependent p-values, and the proof is omitted.
FWER control loses power quickly as m grows (Fig 13.5), but the simulation setting behind it is not specified.
Scheffe's alpha_S and the 'correct' m for post-hoc tests are not derived (footnote 14: technical, out of scope).
The permutation approach assumes X and Y have the same distribution under H0, not just equal means.
Authors note the resampling section is harder and can be skipped; written in 2020, with p-value controversy noted in social science.
FDR thresholds have no standard value; q is context- or dataset-dependent (10% to 30% examples).
practices: Report the p-value itself, not just whether it is below 0.05; avoid blind adherence to 0.05 (footnote 9, p.562).
Default to a two-sided p-value unless only one direction is of scientific interest (footnote 8, p.561).
When many hypotheses are tested, correct for multiplicity; do not reject on raw p<alpha (Sec 13.2).
Use Holm instead of Bonferroni because it is uniformly more powerful and needs no independence assumption (p.568-569).
Use Tukey for all pairwise comparisons of G means and Scheffe for post-hoc linear contrasts, because they beat Bonferroni in those cases (Sec 13.3.2).
Control FWER when m is small (5 or 10) and FDR when m is large and the study is exploratory (Sec 13.3.3, 13.4.1).
Choose the FDR level by the cost of follow-up: about 10% if follow-up is expensive, about 30% if cheap (p.574-575).
Use a permutation null when no theoretical null exists or its assumptions fail (small n, skewed data); trust resampling when it disagrees with the theoretical p-value (footnote 17, Sec 13.5.3).
Use the same set of permutations for all m hypotheses when computing the plug-in FDR (footnote 18).
Do not cherry-pick the smallest p-values before correcting, since FWER and FDR procedures assume all tested hypotheses are adjusted (Exercise 8, p.596).

terms.definition: the probability of observing a test statistic equal to or more extreme than the observed statistic, under the assumption that H0 is in fact true
the probability of making a Type I error given that H0 holds, i.e., the probability of incorrectly rejecting H0
the probability of not making a Type II error given that Ha holds, i.e., the probability of correctly rejecting H0
the probability of making at least one Type I error: FWER = Pr(V >= 1)
sets the threshold for rejecting each hypothesis test to alpha/m, so that FWER <= alpha
order p-values, L = min{j : p(j) > alpha/(m+1-j)}, reject all with p < p(L)
the ratio V/R of false positives to total positives
FDR = E(FDP) = E(V/R); replaced by 0 when R = 0
L = max{j : p(j) < qj/m}; reject all null hypotheses with p <= p(L)
the smallest FDR threshold at which we would reject a particular null hypothesis
a new p-value corrected for multiple testing; reject if it is <= the desired FWER
the known or assumed distribution of the test statistic under H0 (normal, t, chi-squared, F)
estimate FDR by plugging R into the denominator and a resampling estimate of E(V) into the numerator (Algorithm 13.4)

figures.caption: The density function for the N(0, 1) distribution, with the vertical line indicating a value of 2.33.
figures.why: shows the p-value as tail area (T=2.33 gives p=0.02).

figures.caption: The family-wise error rate, as a function of the number of hypotheses tested (displayed on the log scale), for three values of alpha: 0.05, 0.01, 0.001.
figures.why: shows how fast 1-(1-alpha)^m approaches 1; the strongest single picture for the multiplicity problem.

figures.caption: Sorted p-values for tests of m = 10 null hypotheses, m0 = 2 true; Bonferroni (black line) vs Holm (blue line) at FWER 0.05.
figures.why: makes Holm's extra rejections visible against Bonferroni's flat threshold.

figures.caption: Sorted p-values for m = 15 pairwise tests of G = 6 means; Bonferroni vs Tukey vs no adjustment.
figures.why: shows Tukey slightly beats Bonferroni when tests are dependent.

figures.caption: Power as a function of FWER with 90% true nulls, m = 10, 100, 500.
figures.why: shows FWER-power tradeoff and why FWER is poor for large m.

figures.caption: m = 2,000 ordered Fund p-values with Bonferroni (green) and Benjamini-Hochberg (orange) thresholds at 0.05, 0.1, 0.3.
figures.why: side-by-side of FWER and FDR thresholds; best candidate for the hypothesis testing note.

figures.caption: Theoretical vs re-sampling null distribution for the 11th Khan gene (T=-2.09).
figures.why: case where permutation and theory agree.

figures.caption: Theoretical vs re-sampling null distribution for the 877th Khan gene (T=-0.57).
figures.why: case where an outlier makes theory and permutation disagree.

figures.caption: Estimated FDR vs number of rejections for 2,308 Khan genes: BH versus plug-in resampling.
figures.why: shows the two FDR estimates nearly overlap.

figures.caption: 95% confidence intervals for each manager on the Fund data, using Tukey's method.
figures.why: overlapping simultaneous intervals show no significant pairwise difference.

figures.caption: Results of testing m null hypotheses (V, S, U, W, R, m0).
figures.why: defines the V/R notation that FWER and FDR both use.
